subject: Anthropology
title: Double Descent
description: A fast breakdown of Double Descent for builders.

hook.text: You belong to your father's clan for land and your mother's clan for movable property. Two lines, two sets of rules.

buildup.text: Double descent uses both patrilineal and matrilineal principles, assigning different rights through each line.

discovery.text: The Yako of Nigeria inherit land through the father and movable wealth through the mother. Both lines carry duties.

twist.text: Double descent is rare but reveals that descent rules aren't rigid. Cultures can mix systems to serve different needs.

climax.text: Double descent proves that kinship is flexible engineering. Societies design rules to manage property and loyalty.

punchline.text: Two lines of descent, two sets of obligations.

quiz.question: What is double descent?
options: Using both patrilineal and matrilineal descent for different rights
Tracing descent only through the father

details.summary: Double descent systems trace kinship through both matrilineal and patrilineal lines simultaneously but for different purposes. A person may inherit property through their father's line and ritual status through their mother's line.
details.whyItMatters: Double descent shows that kinship systems can be more complex than simple unilineal models suggest. Societies can use multiple descent principles simultaneously to organize different domains of social life.
takeaways: Double descent uses both patrilineal and matrilineal lines simultaneously
Each line governs different aspects like property versus ritual status
The system demonstrates the complexity of kinship organization

faq.question: How does double descent work in practice?
faq.answer: A person belongs to two descent groups simultaneously. Among the Yako of Nigeria, land passes patrilineally while movable wealth passes matrilineally. Each individual has obligations and rights in both lineages for different social domains.

faq.question: Is double descent common across cultures?
faq.answer: No, it is relatively rare. Double descent is found primarily in parts of West Africa and Melanesia. Most societies use a single descent principle — patrilineal, matrilineal, or bilateral — to organize kinship relationships.
